data.title: Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not
data.description:
Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Others would rather have Huang back.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

Nvidia founder’s wife faces spotlight that MacKenzie Scott and Melinda French Gates know well

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

  • Amy Hood, Microsoft’s CFO since 2013, who has managed the company’s massive AI infrastructure spending.
  • Scott Guthrie, who runs Microsoft’s cloud and AI group. Microsoft is a major Nvidia customer.
  • Judson Althoff, whom CEO Satya Nadella named CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business last year, overseeing sales, marketing and operations.

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

data.title: ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox
data.description:
Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

data.title: Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal
data.description:
Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

data.title: ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil
data.description:
If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

Microsoft hasn’t said what caused the outage, which began Thursday morning, but it said it has no evidence of malicious activity.

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.”

Microsoft has promised a full report on the root cause once the problem is resolved.

In the meantime, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

Microsoft hasn’t yet responded to an inquiry from GeekWire about the cause.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”

We’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

data.title: Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1
data.description:
Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.

The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

data.title: Nvidia’s interim CEO spent 13 years at Microsoft, largely out of public view
data.description:
Colette Kress, named Nvidia’s interim CEO on Thursday after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation, spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, including four as chief financial officer of the Redmond company’s Server and Tools business.

But to say she was under the radar would be an understatement: a search of Seattle-area news archives turns up a single mention of her name from her Microsoft years, in a 2007 press release listing her as a presenter at a Hotel 1000 seminar on Microsoft’s budgeting software.

Of course, that’s to be expected. Divisional finance execs aren’t typically public faces at Microsoft or anywhere else. But now she finds herself in the global spotlight, running the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom — at least for the time being.

Nvidia announced Thursday morning that Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, following reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy, and a second affair with a direct report.

Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent CEO, considering internal and external candidates. Director Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys CEO, becomes Nvidia’s first board chair.

Nvidia shares fell more than 13% in early trading.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note Thursday morning that Kress has built “enormous credibility” inside and outside Nvidia.

“We always believed she would eventually be CEO of a major public tech company, but she would have to leave Nvidia after many years there,” he wrote.

Kress joined Microsoft in 1997 after finance roles at Texas Instruments, and held senior positions in corporate planning and finance before becoming chief financial officer of the Server and Tools business, which sold Windows Server, SQL Server and Visual Studio. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as a Microsoft corporate vice president from April 2006 to November 2010.

Server and Tools was also a training ground for Microsoft’s current leadership. Satya Nadella took over the business in 2011, after Kress left, and used it as a springboard to the CEO job three years later. Amy Hood, now Microsoft’s CFO, served as its chief of staff earlier in her career.

From Microsoft, Kress went to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization. Nvidia hired her as CFO in September 2013, ending a search of more than two years.

Now as Nvidia’s interim CEO, her first major test comes quickly. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, Nov. 17, with an earnings call scheduled for 2 p.m. Pacific.
